items.title: AI is now a financing story: $466B borrowed YTD vs $101B a year ago
items.idea: Morgan Stanley/FT: AI companies borrowed $466B by mid-October vs $101B at the same point of 2025. Weekly CDS volume on seven AI names topped $9B in September, 4.5x July. CoreWeave costs $1.09M a year to insure $10M of debt vs $101K for Nvidia. JPM's flows team sees a ~$500B financing gap this year and $696B in 2027 after buybacks and dividends.
items.angle: The CDS curve is the only regulator in this build-out, and it already prices CoreWeave at ~11x Nvidia. Dauber pairs long LRCX vs short ORCL on it.
items.tweetA: $466B of AI borrowing in 10 months vs $101B last year. Credit desks are now charging CoreWeave 11x what they charge Nvidia to insure the same $10M. Nobody in Washington is pricing AI risk that precisely. $CRWV $ORCL $NVDA
items.tweetB: The funding gap is $500B this year and $696B next, and it clears at a 5.13% 10-year. A 4.6x jump in borrowing is not 'AI demand'. It is AI demand that needs someone else's balance sheet to exist.

items.title: Four beats, four sells: Meta, Tesla, IBM, Lam all lower after good prints
items.idea: Meta (rev $64.6B, capex guide $135-145B plus a $9.89B litigation charge), Tesla, IBM and Lam all beat and all got sold. Kospi -3.52%, NQ futures -1.8%. Record $7B of retail money went into SOXL. Dauber's read: investors stopped paying for demand and started charging for the money, though a crowded-long flush is the alternative.
items.angle: When a beat is a sell the market is repricing the cost of capital, not the demand. Watch whether SOXL outflows follow the retail inflow record.
items.tweetA: A record $7B of retail went into SOXL right before four AI-adjacent beats all got sold. That's not a demand scare. That's the marginal buyer finding out what leverage costs. $SOXL $LRCX $META
items.tweetB: Four companies beat and all four traded down. When good news can't lift price, the bid you were relying on was borrowed. Worth asking who's lending it.

items.title: HY at 333bp but CCC at 1,310bp: the dispersion is the signal
items.idea: High yield printed 333bp (+4bp) on a day the Russell gained. CCC is at 1,310bp, a 2026 high, while BB sits near 200bp. Dauber is net short credit and says he is wrong if CCC rallies back through 1,100bp or HY goes to ~290bp with the 10-year above 5.00%.
items.angle: Index spread hides the tail. 1,110bp between CCC and BB is where the AI-adjacent borrowers sit.
items.tweetA: HY index at 333bp looks calm. CCC at 1,310bp is a 2026 high and BB is at 200. The spread between them is 1,100bp. The index is an average of two different markets.
items.tweetB: Everyone quotes the HY OAS. The better question is how many AI borrowers are in the CCC bucket versus BB. Credit already knows the answer.

items.title: Kupperman's 'Project Zimbabwe' vs Perkins' mild-recession wargame
items.idea: Harris Kupperman's Q3 letter: funding gets cut first, neoclouds go bankrupt next, then frontier labs, 'slowly then all at once'; he owns SOFR futures and call spreads. Dario Perkins (TS Lombard) wargames a >=30% equity fall (~$20T market cap), $125-200B credit losses, but only a mild recession, with the capex cycle ending early 2028. Bessent sees no 'systemic problem'. Dauber puts it 60/40 financing vs positioning flush.
items.angle: Two credible people disagree on timing by ~18 months. The tradeable gap is between 'this quarter' and 'early 2028'.
items.tweetA: Kupperman: neoclouds go first, then labs, 'slowly then all at once'. Perkins: -30% equities, $20T gone, mild recession, end of capex cycle early 2028. Both can be right. The only disagreement is whether you're early by 2 years.
items.tweetB: Perkins' base case needs the Fed to have room to cut. With a 5.13% 10-year, December hike odds alive and Brent at $112, the 'long yields fall in a demand shock' leg is the one I'd stress.

items.title: US crude + SPR near 700mb, lowest since 1983; Gulf-Asia freight $38/bbl
items.idea: US crude inventories including SPR are near 700 million barrels, the lowest since 1983. Commercial crude fell 3.06mb vs 0.82mb expected. US Gulf to Asia freight runs ~$38/bbl vs $3-6 pre-war. Brent touched $112.68 but has not settled above $110. Distillates built 1.68mb. Thai rice export prices +37% y/y (Nomura).
items.angle: The delivered barrel is $30+ above the screen. Freight is where the war shows up before the headline price.
items.tweetA: US crude plus SPR near 700mb, lowest since 1983. Freight from the Gulf Coast to Asia is $38/bbl, up from $3-6. The screen says $110. The delivered barrel says a lot more. $XLE $BRENT
items.tweetB: Brent hasn't settled above $110 once, while Thai rice is +37% and Gulf freight is 7x. The market is pricing the paper barrel and ignoring the physical one.

items.title: Gold failed as a haven: -1.2% to $4,102 on seven damaged tankers
items.idea: Gold fell 1.2% to $4,102 at 08:53 ET while seven tankers were reported damaged in Hormuz and Brent rose 2.9%; silver -2.9%. 10-year bid at 5.08%, yen 157.03, DXY 101.53. Dauber reads mixed havens plus risk down as a rotation into duration, not a de-gross. He is short gold; wrong if it closes above its 50-day near $4,358.
items.angle: Gold falling on a war headline with real yields at 5%+ says the marginal haven buyer is a bond fund.
items.tweetA: Seven tankers hit in Hormuz, Brent +2.9%, gold -1.2%. A haven that sells off on the escalation is a rate-sensitive asset with a safe-haven story attached. $GLD $GDX
items.tweetB: Gold at $4,102 with a 5.08% 10-year. It's the same trade as 2022, where gold only worked once real yields stopped rising. They haven't stopped.

items.title: Houthis moving from Saudi oil assets to the southern border; Lavrov in Tehran
items.idea: Simon Hunt reads Lavrov's Tehran visit ('sanctions won't stop us') as Russia refusing to drop Iran and expects Houthis to move from Saudi oil infrastructure toward the kingdom's southern border. Saudi airfields and an Aramco field are under Houthi fire into an eighth month of war. Dec Brent and WTI made new highs; one chartist has $120. Lockheed beat: $7.97 vs $7.52 on $20.7B revenue.
items.angle: Escalation is moving from infrastructure to territory. Defense prints are beating into month eight.
items.tweetA: Eight months in, Houthis are hitting Saudi airfields and an Aramco field, Lavrov is in Tehran saying sanctions won't stop them, and Lockheed beat by 45 cents. The war is now a line item. $LMT $XLE
items.tweetB: Russia is selling the US diesel under a waiver while Lavrov visits Tehran. Washington is financing both sides of the oil problem.

items.title: Michigan sentiment 46.3, current conditions 44.7 (record low), 74% rate policy poor
items.idea: Preliminary Michigan: 46.3 vs 48.1 in Sept, record low 44.8 (May), ~45% below the 83.6 mean. Current conditions 44.7 is the lowest on record; expectations 47.3. Inflation expectations 4.7% (1y) and 3.5% (5y), highest since May. Faith in government economic policy: 74% poor. By party (3m avg): Republicans 119, independents 33, Democrats 8. Empirical Research: equity wealth effect ~125bp of spending growth vs 45bp average.
items.angle: Sentiment is at record lows while spending holds up on top-decile equity wealth. A crack in AI stocks removes that faster than lower rates replace it.
items.tweetA: Michigan current conditions: 44.7, lowest ever. Policy approval: 74% poor. Spending hasn't followed because the top decile is carrying the bottom 60% on equity wealth effect running at 125bp vs 45bp normal. That's one margin call away from changing.
items.tweetB: Independents at 33 vs Republicans 119 vs Democrats 8. When the marginal voter and the marginal consumer are the same person, sentiment data stops being soft data.

items.title: Pending home sales -7.3% to 66.0, lowest since the series began in 2001
items.idea: Pending home sales fell 7.3% in September to 66.0, the lowest since 2001, all four regions down. Builder sentiment at 29 is below every starts reading since 2012. 30-year mortgage rate 7.41% (from 7.50%), yet purchase applications still fell 7.3%.
items.angle: A 9bp mortgage rate improvement did nothing. Housing is the visible transmission channel for a 5% 10-year.
items.tweetA: 30-year mortgage rate eased to 7.41%. Purchase apps fell 7.3% anyway. Pending sales at 66.0 are the lowest in a series that started in 2001. Rate relief at this level doesn't unlock anything.
items.tweetB: Housing was the collateral in 2008. In 2026 it's the one asset class that has repriced and stopped transacting. Note who is not talking about it.

items.title: Claims 194K, a three-month low, keeps the December hike alive
items.idea: Jobless claims 194K vs 200K expected, a three-month low. This keeps December hike odds alive and the front end from following the 10-year lower. Blackstone Q3 distributable earnings fell 9.2% y/y on slower dealmaking; Huntington and Sallie Mae report.
items.angle: Labor holding while sentiment collapses is the stagflationary setup: no cut cushion from weakness.
items.tweetA: Claims at 194K, sentiment at record lows, Brent at $112, the Fed debating a hike. The labor market is the only thing that hasn't gotten the memo. $TLT $SPY
items.tweetB: Blackstone distributable earnings -9.2% on slower deals while claims fall to a 3-month low. Private markets are slowing before the labor market notices.

items.title: Policy fly-swallowing: red-dye diesel for truckers led to an $8B farmer fund
items.idea: Iran/Ukraine cut diesel supply. The administration suspended the restriction on truckers buying tax-free red-dye diesel. Farmers now compete for that fuel, so an $8B assistance fund followed. Dauber: secondary and tertiary effects are underestimated and each fix generates the next problem.
items.angle: Each relief program sits on top of the previous inflation. Fiscal cost lands at the long end.
items.tweetA: Step 1: diesel spikes. Step 2: truckers get red-dye diesel. Step 3: farmers lose supply. Step 4: $8B farmer fund. That's a policy ladder, and it ends at the 30-year.
items.tweetB: Nobody scored the $8B fund against the federal diesel tax that was deferred, not eliminated. The real cost is a 2027 tax liability and a 5% 30-year paying for it.

items.title: p(doom) above 10% and no FAA: the regulation analogy
items.idea: Dauber cannot square CEO-stated p(doom) >10% with opposition to federal or state regulation. Nuclear got the AEC/NRC; airlines have the FAA/NTSB; food and pharma have regulators. 'Money is talking, loudly.'
items.angle: The regulatory capture vs safety debate is now mainstream among market writers, not just AI people.
items.tweetA: Delta can't self-inspect its planes. Pharma can't release its own drugs. AI labs publish their own p(doom) above 10% and lobby against oversight. Name another industry that gets that deal.
items.tweetB: The AEC came after Hiroshima. The question for AI is whether the FAA moment comes before the crash or after.

items.title: SpaceX revenue +161% to $14.6B; AI is 52% of it; Tesla merger floated
items.idea: SpaceX revenue +161% to $14.6B, AI now 52% of revenue ahead of connectivity at 36%. Musk called a Tesla merger 'a good idea' the day Tesla cut capex outlook to ~$20B from $25B and slid Optimus. SpaceX 5-year CDS at a record $226K per $10M (FT).
items.angle: SpaceX was paid for AI revenue, Tesla punished for cutting AI capex. A merger would put cash flow and spend on one balance sheet.
items.tweetA: SpaceX: AI is 52% of $14.6B revenue, connectivity 36%. It is a compute company with rockets, and its CDS is at a record. Tesla cuts capex and gets sold. Musk wants to merge them. $TSLA
items.tweetB: Tesla cut capex 20% and was punished. SpaceX raised AI spend and was paid. Merging them is the market's own answer to which one it wants to own.

items.title: Diesel crack at ~$100/bbl, 5x normal; NYH diesel hit ~$230 in September
items.idea: NYH diesel futures hit an all-time high near $230/bbl in September, more than 2x crude. The crack spread is ~$100 vs a normal ~$20. Seaborne diesel exports from the largest suppliers are down 1-1.5mbpd against ~30mbpd demand. Middle East refined product exports are below half of pre-war. US refinery utilisation is ~94%.
items.angle: A 1-1.5mbpd shortfall on 30mbpd demand makes a $100 crack. That's what a 4% supply gap does in an inelastic market.
items.tweetA: Diesel supply is short 1-1.5mbpd on 30mbpd demand: a 4% gap. The crack spread is 5x normal. That's the price of inelastic demand, and it's why refiners are the cleanest war trade. $VLO $MPC $PSX
items.tweetB: Diesel at $200+/bbl wholesale and $6 at the pump weeks before the midterms. The voter reads it at the pump, the Fed reads it in core goods. Both are reading the same barrel.

items.title: Europe slow-played the IEA release: ~100 of 400mb still unreleased
items.idea: The IEA noted ~100mb of the record 400mb March release has not been released. The G7 promised a 'frontloaded substantial diesel release within 20 days'; it has been 18 days with nothing tangible. A 50mb release over four months would cover roughly one-third of the lost supply. US and Japan largely fulfilled their crude-heavy commitments.
items.angle: A coordinated reserve release is a policy promise with a delivery lag. Delivery risk is a price risk for heating oil this winter.
items.tweetA: 400mb pledged in March, ~100mb undelivered. The G7 promised diesel in 20 days, day 18 and nothing. If a winter shortfall happens, the story won't be supply. It'll be that Europe held back stocks for 'real' shortages while prices called it one.
items.tweetB: 50mb over four months is a third of what's missing. Even if Europe delivers everything it promised, the market is still short. The release only reduces the size of the hole.

items.title: Waiver on Russian diesel to Apr 2027 while Ukraine keeps hitting refineries
items.idea: Treasury waived sanctions on Russian diesel through April 7, 2027 after Putin pledged 500kt in November (~125kbpd). Russian diesel/gasoil exports have collapsed from just under 1mbpd to 100-150kbpd, so the pledge is either the status quo or a doubling. Trump's 'energy ceasefire' became, per a White House official, a 'refinery for refinery proposal'. Ukraine hit Ryazan; Zelensky: 'we're done.'
items.angle: Sanctions relief funds the Russian windfall Ukraine's refinery strikes are designed to deny. The incentives are opposed.
items.tweetA: The US waives sanctions on Russian diesel while Ukraine bombs Russian refineries to deny the money. 500kt is 125kbpd, which is roughly where exports already were. The deal buys headlines, not barrels.
items.tweetB: Washington needs Russian diesel and Kyiv needs Russia not to have it. The White House has to choose which ally it is asking to stand down.

items.title: Meta capex +80% y/y to $34.9B on 26% revenue growth; SMCI pre-announces $4B beat
items.idea: Meta revenue +26% to $64.6B vs $63.3B consensus; capex $34.9B in Q3, +80% from $19.4B, 2026 low end raised to $135B. Super Micro pre-announced Sept quarter revenue of $18.5-19.5B vs guidance of $14.5-15.5B, a ~$4B raise at the midpoint. SpaceX AI computing revenue was strong. S&P closed +0.58% Wednesday.
items.angle: Capex +80% against revenue +26% means the gap is being financed. Same day, Dauber says investors started charging for the money. Opposite readings of the same prints.
items.tweetA: Meta: revenue +26%, capex +80%. SMCI raised the quarter by $4B in a pre-announcement. Both can be true: demand is real and the capex growth rate is running 3x revenue. $META $SMCI
items.tweetB: Wednesday the tape rallied on SMCI and SpaceX. Thursday morning it sold Meta, Tesla, IBM and Lam. Same data, 24 hours apart. The AI trade is now a daily referendum on the cost of capital.

items.title: The 5.00% HY OAS line: 2.59% low to 3.33% now; junk yield 8.26%
items.idea: ICE BofA HY OAS jumped from 2.59% to 3.33%. His warning threshold is 5.00%, where late-2018 and 2022 topped out; March 2020 peaked at 10.87%. B-rated junk yield rose from ~6.5% in January to 8.26%, highest since late 2023, and in recent weeks the 10-year fell while junk yield kept rising, so the move is spread not rates. S&P closed a record 7,757 on Oct 21.
items.angle: Equities at records with junk yield at a 3-year high is the divergence. His rule: real drawdown starts when junk yield spikes, not grinds.
items.tweetA: S&P at a record 7,757. B-rated junk yield at 8.26%, the highest since late 2023, and the 10-year has been falling. That is spread widening, not rates. The two charts don't agree. One of them is wrong.
items.tweetB: HY OAS +74bp from the low to 3.33%. Altrichter's tripwire is 5.00%. That's another +167bp. In 2018 and 2022 that took 3-4 months. Ask what the current setup needs to get there.

items.title: MOVE index 80 to 114 to 96; Capital One provisions $700M below estimates
items.idea: MOVE jumped from ~80 mid-September to ~114 in early October and eased to 95.94 on Oct 21. 10-year broke below 5.20% support and sits at 5.04%. Capital One beat; credit loss provisions were $700M below estimates, supporting the 'stable consumer' view from JPM. COF's book skews to lower-quality borrowers.
items.angle: COF provisioning low while Michigan prints record-low current conditions. Spending and sentiment are decoupled.
items.tweetA: Capital One set aside $700M less than expected for bad loans. Michigan current conditions: record low. Subprime-skewed card book says consumer is fine. The survey says the opposite. One of them is lagging. $COF
items.tweetB: MOVE went 80 to 114 and back to 96 in five weeks. Rate vol spiked and mean-reverted, and credit spreads didn't. Bond vol is the first thing to calm in a regime change.

items.title: NQ -700 pts, VIX +15%: QQQ under the 100-day, 200-day 'wouldn't shock me'
items.idea: SPY gapped under the 50-day again; NQ down 700+ points, VIX +15%. He says the market hated Meta's financial situation and potential cash raise. QQQ is below its 100-day and a touch of the 200-day is plausible; 6-month Nasdaq uptrend lost. Scanners show few tech momentum leaders, only a handful of SaaS.
items.angle: Technical read: tech has lost its 6-month trend and momentum scanners show no tech leaders. Rotation is the story (see Bespoke Staples).
items.tweetA: NQ -700, VIX +15%, QQQ through the 100-day. The momentum scanner has almost no tech names. When the leadership screen is empty of the leading sector, the trend isn't pausing. $QQQ $SPY
items.tweetB: The 200-day is 'where markets usually bottom or things get much worse'. That's the honest framing. The chart doesn't say which.

items.title: Anthropic merges 30,000 changes/day, up from 2,500 in May: 12x in four months
items.idea: From Anthropic's engineering blog: ~2,500 merged changes/day in May 2026, over 30,000/day by September. 25M git checkouts/day, mostly CI; ~3,000 staff each running 10-15 parallel agents; monorepo working copy 25GB. Gergely: output of a 3,500-person company looks like 35,000-70,000 engineers. 'Coding is no longer the bottleneck'; source control, builds and CI are.
items.angle: The bottleneck moved from writing code to merging, building and testing it. That's a compute and infra demand curve nobody modelled.
items.tweetA: 2,500 merged changes/day in May. 30,000 in September. 10 per engineer per day across ~3,000 staff. The constraint isn't writing code anymore, it's CI, builds and source control. Wonder whose capex that shows up in.
items.tweetB: A 3,500-person firm doing the output of a 35-70K-person one. Multiply that across every software shop and ask what happens to seat-based SaaS pricing and to the 'cost of an engineer' in every comp model.

items.title: Scion: seven engineers, Rust, Spanner, 100% of the monorepo off Git
items.idea: Anthropic built Scion (server and client in Rust, changesets in Google Spanner, blobs in Cloud Storage), plus Antique for code review (Go + React). Seven engineers maintain it. 100% of the monorepo is off Git; Claude helped with the migration, 'force the cutover at 99% coverage and let Claude fix what mattered'. Autoscaling hasn't been needed through 10x merge growth. Mononoke's creator alleges a copy; Anthropic added attribution after complaint.
items.angle: Agent-scale engineering orgs will rebuild their dev infra. Git-compatible vendors (Entire, Cursor Origin, Code Storage) are the picks and shovels.
items.tweetA: Seven engineers replaced Git for the lab that merges 30K changes a day. Claude did much of the migration. The headcount-to-leverage ratio inside these companies isn't a projection, it's a payroll fact.
items.tweetB: Cutting over at 99% coverage and letting the model fix what mattered is a new migration doctrine. Most enterprises run the opposite, 5-year dual-run programs.

items.title: Git replacement is a market: Entire, Cursor Origin, Code Storage; Ball: open source 'doesn't make sense'
items.idea: A new batch of vendors position as git-compatible version control for AI scale: Entire (Thomas Dohmke, GitHub's last CEO), Cursor Origin by SpaceX, and Code Storage by The Pierre Company. Thorsten Ball (Amp) predicts open source doesn't make sense in its current form anymore. Gergely guesses few companies will build their own VCS.
items.angle: A venture category forming around the new bottleneck: agent-scale developer infrastructure.
items.tweetA: Git was designed for offline laptops. AI shops are always online with 10-15 agents per engineer. Three startups are betting that mismatch is a category. GitHub's last CEO is one of them.
items.tweetB: If code is cheap and merge throughput is the constraint, what does open source even mean? Thorsten Ball's take is that it breaks. I'd want to know what that does to the licensing economics.

items.title: Abbott as acquirer of Biodesix: Perceptive PIK loan at SOFR+9%, 5% prepay premium dropping to 2% after Nov 21
items.idea: BDSX (market cap ~$252M) debt: 1-month SOFR with 3% floor +9% (12.88% now), secured on IP, lender Perceptive, interest rolls up and pays at Nov 2028 maturity. Early payback premium 5%, falling to 2% after Nov 21, 2026 and gone May 21, 2027. Perceptive holds warrants for 375K shares at $8.38-$12.93. TD Cowen $40 PT (Oct 13). Jack Schuler (85, ex-Abbott COO) owns a large stake in an estate-planning annuity. Revenue +34%, diagnostics +42%.
items.angle: The financing structure is built to be taken out. The prepay premium step-down is a dated catalyst.
items.tweetA: Biodesix has a PIK loan at SOFR+9% with a 5% prepay premium that steps to 2% on Nov 21 and zero by May. That's a debt schedule written for a takeout. Abbott's CEO keeps saying 'tuck-in'. $BDSX $ABT
items.tweetB: Abbott's CEO bought St Jude, ran a tuck-in playbook, then bought Exact for $22B and said the same. BDSX is the only working lung-nodule blood test. The market cap is $252M. The thesis is one sentence.

items.title: Lung nodules: Nodify moves 66 vs 24 patients into 'likely benign', invasive procedures 5% vs 19%
items.idea: In the PANOPTIC trial (178 patients, 29 cancers), doctors alone classified 24 as likely benign, 3 of whom had cancer. With Nodify, 66 are likely benign, only 1 had cancer. In ORACLE, invasive procedures in benign nodules were 5% with XL2-informed care vs 19% usual care. Pneumothorax after needle biopsy happens 15-28% of the time. CHEST has now included biomarker tests as an adjunct in nodule guidelines.
items.angle: Test value is a base-rate game: a modest AUC improvement avoids a 15-28% complication risk in people with 10% cancer odds.
items.tweetA: Needle biopsy causes a collapsed lung 15-28% of the time. If you're 10% likely to have cancer, that's a bad trade. A blood test that moves 66 of 178 patients to 'watch' instead of 24 changes the math. CHEST just wrote it into guidelines.
items.tweetB: Exact Sciences tried to build a nodule test and failed in a trial. Guardant tried and has nothing. There's one working product. In diagnostics, 'only one that works' is a moat.

items.title: JPM and Citi block outside AI agents; IBKR and Robinhood let them trade
items.idea: JPMorgan restricts outside agents' access to customer accounts; Citi bars outside agents from logging in or transacting. Interactive Brokers launched AI-powered autonomous trading and Robinhood lets customers authorise agents to trade. Matt's explanation: liability. Banks hold deposits; brokerages offer accounts designed for risk. Compares it to driverless cars circa 2015.
items.angle: Agent-to-broker is the first live agentic-finance split. Banks are gatekeeping, brokers are monetising.
items.tweetA: Citi and JPM won't let outside AI agents log in. Robinhood and IBKR will let them trade. The divide isn't about technology, it's about who has to make the customer whole when the agent is wrong.
items.tweetB: A bank is liable for the deposit. A broker is liable for suitability. Agents sit in the first category when they move money and the second when they place trades. That's why the line is where it is.

items.title: RavenPack distilled Nemotron 120B into a 4B model: 39x throughput, 96% label match; Santander €5 to €0.03
items.idea: RavenPack used Nvidia's 120B Nemotron 3 Super to label financial text, then fine-tuned a 4B Nemotron 3 Nano on those labels. It labeled 845K+ excerpts in under an hour at 39x the throughput and matched the larger model on ~96% of sentence-level labels. Santander says specialised models cut serving costs from €5 to €0.03.
items.angle: Distillation is the cost curve story: a 100x cut in cost per task for a 4% accuracy gap. Bespoke datasets become cheaper than vendor datasets.
items.tweetA: 120B model labels the data, 4B model learns from it, runs 39x faster and agrees 96% of the time. Santander says €5 down to €0.03 per serve. That's a 166x cost cut. Pricing power in data vendors is next.
items.tweetB: If a hedge fund can build a custom 'pricing power' dataset in an hour for a few dollars, what exactly is the premium on a $200K alt-data feed paying for?

items.title: FCA, UK Pensions Regulator, CFTC (Oct 28) and BoE all moving on AI at once
items.idea: FCA wants disclaimers on AI financial advice, reporting of significant AI failures and near-misses, work on agent identity and accountability; supervisors found overstated capabilities and weak monitoring. UK Pensions Regulator told trustees to test diversification against an AI downturn. CFTC Oct 28 roundtable on autonomous trading agents and compute markets. BoE considers stress-testing AI's effect on finance over herding risk.
items.angle: Four regulators, one week, same worry: correlated agent behaviour. That's the Oct 15 de-gross problem, but automated.
items.tweetA: FCA, UK Pensions Regulator, CFTC, and the BoE all moved on AI this week. The Pensions Regulator is asking trustees whether their diversification survives an AI downturn. That's the question I'd put to every allocator. $SPY
items.tweetB: The BoE's worry is herding when models respond to a shock the same way. Hedge funds already did that on Oct 15 without agents. Add agents and it happens in seconds.

items.title: Qualitate raises $25M for AI interviewers; Tradeweb buys Trumid $1.97B
items.idea: Qualitate raised $25M led by Insight Partners to use AI agents to conduct interviews at scale; Heron Intelligence calls experts post-earnings. Tradeweb to acquire Trumid for $1.97B. AI helped an ex-Citadel trader's hedge fund post 6% in September. Hackers used Grok and Claude to attack LatAm banks (PYMNTS).
items.angle: Primary research is getting a marginal cost near zero. Expert networks are the exposed business model.
items.tweetA: AI interviewers can run thousands of expert calls after every earnings print. Expert-network margins assume a human on the phone for $1,000/hr. Qualitate just raised $25M to test that.
items.tweetB: Tradeweb paying $1.97B for Trumid says electronic credit trading is consolidating at the exact moment credit gets interesting. Timing is not an accident.

items.source: Paul Podolsky / A Letter from Paul
items.title: G20 has delivered 16 quarter-point hikes; gold fell first, then bonds, Europe, US credit, now US stocks
items.idea: Liquidity tightening amid more issuance: 16 quarter-point hikes within the G20, falling prices, large deficits, plus private debt and share issuance (CoreWeave bonds, SpaceX IPO). The sequence: gold fell first, then bonds, European stocks, US corporate credit, now US stocks. This continues until risky assets fall enough to slow growth and force easing. 'We are not close to that yet.'
items.angle: A sequenced repricing is a map. Gold, bonds, Europe, credit, equities. If it holds, the next step is growth.
items.tweetA: Gold fell first. Then bonds. Then Europe. Then US credit. Now US equities. 16 G20 hikes so far. Podolsky's point is that tightening plus issuance takes down one asset class at a time until something breaks. Which one is left?
items.tweetB: SpaceX IPO and CoreWeave bonds are supply. Supply into a tightening is the textbook mistake. The sequence says equities are the last domino, not the first.

items.title: AI stocks at 17-18x P/E that 'should trade at 10': two articles of faith
items.idea: AI-linked companies that would normally trade at 10x now trade at 17-18x because of two assumptions: compute demand is unlimited, supply is constrained. He says both are wrong. Frontier model demand depends on creditors giving hundreds of billions to OpenAI; falling costs per token erode Nvidia's moat. SpaceX runs out of money in six months without more borrowing yet pitches the whole US economy as TAM.
items.angle: Falling cost is the bear case for the moat, even if demand rises. Jevons works for volume but not for margin.
items.tweetA: Two articles of faith keep AI at 17-18x P/E: unlimited demand, constrained supply. Demand rises because costs fall. Falling costs aren't good for the moat. Both can't hold at a 17x. $NVDA
items.tweetB: 'If creditors don't give hundreds of billions to OpenAI soon, its demand will slow.' That's a funding problem written as a demand problem. Dauber, Podolsky and the CDS curve are all in the same place.

items.source: Paul Podolsky / A Letter from Paul
items.title: Escalation template: tariffs 10% became 20-100%+; Iran 'surgical' became protracted; Nov 3
items.idea: Podolsky: at each juncture the White House escalates. Tariffs expected ~10% went to 20-100%+, border enforcement moved far from the border, Iran was supposed to be surgical and became protracted. Applying the same template to Nov 3, he expects an effort to disrupt a vote the White House is forecast to lose, possibly with an Iran escalation. He's positioned for all three forces to worsen.
items.angle: Pattern-based political risk. The market has no vol premium on a contested election.
items.tweetA: Tariffs: expected 10%, delivered 20-100%+. Iran: 'surgical', now 8 months. Podolsky applies the same template to Nov 3. I have no view on the politics. I do have a view that nobody is paying for a vol premium on the downside of this pattern.
items.tweetB: Approval at the low of either term, record-low sentiment, diesel at $6, Nov 3 weeks away. The market is pricing none of it, and VIX is at 15% higher on a day.

items.title: Altcoin entry rule: only buy support if the coin held up vs BTC over 7 days (-10% vs BTC -6% ok, -18% no)
items.idea: Mark daily support levels, compare 7-day relative performance to BTC on CoinGecko, and place bids just above support only if the alt showed relative strength. If BTC is -6% and the alt -10%, still fine; at -18% he waits. NEAR example: levels at $3.526 and $4.562. He frames BTC at $87K vs $81K as unimportant but alt entry price as critical.
items.angle: A simple relative-strength filter. A rule is checkable, which makes it content.
items.tweetA: A rule I'd actually use: only bid an alt at support if it fell less than ~1.7x BTC over the week. BTC -6%, alt -10% passes. Alt -18% means it hasn't found its bottom. Works in either direction.
items.tweetB: Relative strength vs BTC in a drawdown is the cheapest proxy for who's holding the coin. Weak holders sell first, so a coin falling 3x BTC still has sellers left.

items.title: a16z renames its crypto fund 'a16z Frontier' - the label 'crypto' no longer describes what's being built
items.idea: a16z expands its new fund from crypto to frontier startups and renames a16z Crypto to a16z Frontier. 'Wall Street and fintech companies now launch products on blockchains. Does that make them crypto companies?' Themes: native AI use cases (brand-new activities), full-stack startups combining software, hardware, services, networks built for machines that start single-player and become multiplayer, and crypto as money rails for machine-to-machine payments.
items.angle: The biggest crypto VC rebrands away from crypto. Either infrastructure has receded, or crypto narrative alpha is gone.
items.tweetA: a16z just renamed its crypto fund 'Frontier'. Read it two ways: crypto won so completely it's invisible, or the LP appetite for the word is gone. Both are bullish for stablecoin rails and bearish for tokens.
items.tweetB: 'Networks built for machines will look very different.' The machine-to-machine payments thesis is where this fund lands. That needs fast, cheap, programmable money. It doesn't need a token.

items.title: Same announcement, crypto angle: 'infrastructure has receded into the background'; stablecoins the standard tool
items.idea: From the Frontier feed: blockchains have become more widely used and the lines have blurred; stablecoins are quickly becoming a standard tool for fintechs and institutions; because blockchains are programmable, both centralised and decentralised financial services can be built on them. They will 'continue to invest in crypto and advocate for sensible regulation'. Leads: the firm's founders, Eddy Lazzarin, Guy Wuollet.
items.angle: The words 'stablecoins' and 'machine-to-machine' appear; 'token' doesn't. Read the omission.
items.tweetA: Count the words in a16z's Frontier post: stablecoins, rails, machine-to-machine, programmable. Tokens, DeFi yield, memecoins: missing. The crypto allocation in the largest crypto fund just shifted to payments plumbing. $COIN $CRCL
items.tweetB: Fund renames are LP signals. Allocators who couldn't hold 'crypto' can hold 'frontier'. This is a distribution decision as much as a thesis.

items.title: Intel's CTO: today's tool stock supports ~2x leading-edge wafers, not 10x; AI compute has grown 3x a year
items.idea: Pushkar Ranade (Intel CTO): not 10x, 'probably 2x' of leading-edge wafer output possible with the world's existing tools. AI compute has grown ~3x per year for a decade. ASML makes fewer than 100 EUV tools a year and doesn't plan significantly more by decade-end. Peter Wennink (ASML) in the intro clip: demand is 'easily 40-50% above our maximum capacity'. Intel is locked to a specific tool per process once a flow is set (18A).
items.angle: Compute demand compounds at 3x; wafer supply caps at 2x in total. Something has to give: price or efficiency.
items.tweetA: AI compute: 3x a year for a decade. Intel's CTO says the world's installed tool base can double leading-edge wafers, full stop. Do the math on how many years that's good for. It's less than one. $ASML $TSM $INTC
items.tweetB: ASML builds under 100 EUV machines a year and won't build many more this decade. Everyone in the stack is locked to a tool and a supplier. That's the cleanest supply bottleneck in the AI chain.

items.title: $2B of fab capex yields logic for ~$100B of AI-lab revenue: 'virtually vertically integrated'
items.idea: Dwarkesh's math: a couple of billion dollars of capex on Intel's account yields logic enough for ~$100B of model-company revenue per year. Ranade: the industry moved from fully vertical to horizontal (foundry, equipment, suppliers) and is now going 'virtually vertically integrated' as every hyperscaler designs chips and some model companies could consume an entire fab, or several. Early signs of buyers guaranteeing future volumes already exist.
items.angle: A 50x revenue-to-capex leverage on the foundry means value capture sits at the top of the stack, which makes foundry pricing power the optionality.
items.tweetA: $2B of foundry capex enables ~$100B of AI revenue per year. 50x. That's why the AI labs will eventually just write a check for fab capacity. The foundries are underpricing the thing that makes them valuable.
items.tweetB: Intel's CTO says some model companies could consume an entire fab's output on their own. The customer concentration risk that used to worry foundry investors is now the demand signal.

items.title: Terafab: Intel working with Musk; High-NA litho at $400M; fab cost doubling every 4-5 years
items.idea: Intel partners with Elon Musk on 'Terafab' to accelerate a new fab. Ranade: fab costs double every 4-5 years; litho cost doubles faster. A High-NA EUV scanner and associated equipment is ~$400M. He asks whether clean rooms and the process flow itself are indoctrination, and points to 'radically different' approaches. Power, water and consumables are also constraints beyond tools.
items.angle: If patterning cost doubles every few years, a $800M litho step is the end of the road for the status quo.
items.tweetA: A High-NA scanner is ~$400M. Fab cost doubles every 4-5 years. Extend the line and patterning is $800M in four years. Intel's CTO is openly asking if you still need a clean room. That's not a normal thing for a CTO to say. $INTC $TSLA
items.tweetB: Terafab means Musk is buying his way into a fab the way he built rockets: by questioning whether the process was ever necessary. If it works the capex curve bends. If it doesn't, Intel gets paid anyway.

items.title: Why FinFET (1989 demo) took until 2011 and gate-all-around (1988) until 2022; 10nm slipped 2016 to 2018
items.idea: Gate-all-around was demonstrated in 1988, FinFET in 1989; FinFET reached volume production at Intel in 2011, and GAA at Samsung in 2022: a ~decade lag between lab and fab. 10nm's target was 2016, delivered 2018, partly because Intel skipped EUV and 'hyperscaled' without new tools. TSMC started EUV in volume in 2019, ~4 years ahead of Intel's first EUV product in 2023. Chris Auth: don't put too much innovation in one node; phase-gate maturity metrics.
items.angle: A technology that exists in a lab in 1988 can need 34 years to reach mass production. That's the planning horizon for backside power, CFET and 2D materials.
items.tweetA: GAA transistor demonstrated in a lab in 1988. First volume production: 2022. 34 years. Hybrid bonding, CFET and 2D materials are in the same pipeline now. The chips of 2045 are mostly invented already.
items.tweetB: Intel skipped EUV on 10nm and lost four years of tool experience to TSMC. The cost of being wrong about one tool was a decade of market share. Worth remembering when somebody says a technology is 'not ready'.

items.title: Oct 15: fundamental, systematic and multi-strat funds all lost together as AI/tech was de-grossed
items.idea: Fundamental long-short, systematic long-short and multi-strategy platforms all suffered unusually large losses on Oct 15 as crowded tech/AI exposures were cut. De-grossing sells longs and covers shorts at once, so crowded longs fall and popular shorts rise. Example: $300M long / $300M short, longs -5%, shorts -1% = -$12M with zero net exposure on $600M gross.
items.angle: Net exposure said zero. Gross exposure said $600M. Different research processes converge on the same positions at the exposure level.
items.tweetA: A fund with $300M long and $300M short is 'market neutral'. Longs -5%, shorts -1% and it's down $12M. On Oct 15 that happened to fundamental, systematic and multi-strat funds at the same time. Neutral isn't the same as safe. $SPY
items.tweetB: Three different research processes, one position: the semi name that's high on earnings revisions, momentum and a relative-value pod trade. That's why diversification disappeared on the same day.

items.title: IMF: hedge funds hold ~$13T gross assets, >$40T notional; crowded names get deeper drawdowns
items.idea: The IMF estimates hedge funds control ~$13T in gross assets, rising above $40T notional including derivatives. IMF finds stocks with the highest exposure to crowded hedge-fund ownership have materially higher volatility and deeper drawdowns in stress than less crowded ones. Crowded ownership contributes little to calm-market returns, so historical risk models don't estimate it.
items.angle: Ownership itself is a risk factor, and it's invisible in a covariance matrix estimated in calm markets.
items.tweetA: IMF: $13T of hedge fund gross assets, $40T+ notional. The stocks most owned by crowded hedge funds draw down hardest in stress. Your risk model doesn't see it because crowding only shows up on the day it matters.
items.tweetB: Covariance is estimated on data where crowding did nothing. Then it does everything for a week. A factor with zero historical significance and 100% of the loss is the definition of a model gap.

items.title: Fed balance sheet $900B to $6.7T; G4 from ~$4T to $20T+: 'debasement is not inflation'
items.idea: Excerpt from The Everything Code (out Nov 3). Fed balance sheet was ~$900B before 2008, ~$6.7T now after attempted reduction (peak ~$9T); G4 balance sheets grew from ~$4T in 2008 to over $20T by 2024. Total debt/GDP approaching 370% in 2008; household debt ~100% of GDP fell to ~75% while government and corporate debt compounded. Pal's thesis: QE was monetisation, and debasement raises scarce-asset prices (equities, real estate, gold, art) without raising wages or earnings.
items.angle: A clean statement of the 'denominator' thesis. Compare to today's falling gold and rising real yields.
items.tweetA: Pal's claim: QE was never temporary, it was debasement. Fed balance sheet $900B to $6.7T. G4 $4T to $20T+. Fine. Then explain why gold is down on the day it should be the cleanest debasement trade, with a 5%+ 10-year.
items.tweetB: Bernanke in 2011: QE is 'temporary' and the balance sheet 'will be normalized'. The Fed is at 7x its pre-crisis size. Every time a central bank says temporary, the burden of proof should be on them.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (BofA derivatives research)
items.title: BofA: cheapest crash insurance is CADUSD downside puts, not equity options; credit pricing can fund equity protection
items.idea: Bank of America derivatives research flags a disconnect between rising credit-market stress and the relatively low price investors pay for protection elsewhere. Cheapest protection against a serious dislocation may sit in FX (CADUSD downside puts) instead of equity options; a historical comparison of crashes shows differences between hedges that look good over two decades and those that worked in the recent regime. BofA also identifies using credit pricing to finance equity protection, with caveats. (Body truncated in the email.)
items.angle: Hedging across asset classes where vol is mispriced relative to credit stress. CAD as a risk-off proxy.
items.tweetA: Credit stress is rising and equity-option protection is still not cheap. BofA says one of the cheapest crash hedges is CADUSD downside puts. The cleaner question is what that currency actually hedges. $FXC
items.tweetB: Using credit-market pricing to finance equity protection is a funding trade. It works until credit and equities fall together, and that is what the hedge is for.

items.title: Anthropic S-1 reportedly shows an $80B+ net loss this year ahead of IPO
items.idea: As Anthropic prepares to file for an IPO, its S-1 reportedly revealed a net loss above $80B for the year (via ZeroHedge). Blocmates asks how realistic the path to profitability is for AI products. Same issue: Anthropic launched Claude Duet, a proactive agent app that can buy things for your business using Stripe's Link wallet.
items.angle: An $80B annual loss is a funding claim on the same $466B borrowing wave. It's the demand side of the financing gap.
items.tweetA: An $80B net loss in one year in the S-1. Plot it next to $466B of AI borrowing YTD. The IPO is the take-out for that funding gap. The question for public markets is whether they want to be the lender of last resort.
items.tweetB: Revenue is growing faster than any enterprise software company in history and the loss is $80B. Both are true. The question is whether losses scale with revenue or with compute.

items.title: 'Worst day for cybersecurity': Railway hack, eMudhra scandal, tampered Ledgers on four marketplaces
items.idea: 'Everything is hackable.' Railway was hit; yesterday the eMudhra scandal; more tampered Ledger devices found on Lazada Thailand, Amazon Japan, Yahoo Flea Market Japan and Ozon Russia (Mark Karpeles says Ledger knew about the implants in March). Hackers reportedly used Claude and Grok to automate attacks on 400+ banks and financial targets in Latin America. Arkham stopped providing full history, labeling and filtering for non-enterprise users.
items.angle: Supply-chain hardware tampering plus AI-automated attacks: attack cost curve falling faster than defense.
items.tweetA: Tampered Ledgers on Amazon Japan and Lazada. AI-automated attacks on 400+ LatAm banks. A cloud platform hack on the same day. Cost of attacks falls with the model. Cost of defence doesn't. $CRWD $PANW
items.tweetB: A hardware wallet with a pre-installed implant sold through legitimate marketplaces is the full chain: supply, distribution, trust. Self-custody has a logistics problem now.

items.title: 1.7M BTC sits in addresses with exposed public keys; quantum attack estimates fell 20x (Starknet)
items.idea: Starknet says ~1.7M BTC sits in addresses with exposed public keys, with quantum attack resource estimates down 20x. Same issue: Claude traced the NSA-supplied seeds behind NIST's P-256 curve, a 25-year-old cryptographic mystery, in under 30 minutes, and 'Claude Mythos' designed efficient quantum circuits (via X posts).
items.angle: Quantum risk timelines are compressing while AI is cracking old crypto puzzles. It is a tail risk for BTC's security model.
items.tweetA: 1.7M BTC in addresses with exposed public keys. Quantum resource estimates down 20x. An AI model traced P-256's seeds in 30 minutes. Bitcoin's threat model was written before any of those three were true. $BTC
items.tweetB: 20x lower quantum cost estimates doesn't mean 20x sooner. It means the date moves from 'never' to 'a number'. Markets price a date differently from never.

items.title: GENIUS Act rules finalised by OCC, effective Jan 2027; Visa-Mesh to 175M merchants; 73% of stablecoin volume off-hours
items.idea: OCC finalised GENIUS Act rules effective January 2027. Visa and Mesh partnership to make stablecoin and crypto balances spendable at 175M merchants. Coinbase research: 73% of stablecoin volume moves on nights, weekends and holidays. Crypto lending vaults >$10B (from $4B at start of last year, FT). Solana's Alpenglow went live: finality 12s to 150ms. Stripe and Plasma launch multi-currency crypto cards. Deutsche Bank launches crypto custody in Germany.
items.angle: Regulation, merchant distribution and off-hours settlement: all three legs of a stablecoin payments stack arrive in the same week.
items.tweetA: 73% of stablecoin volume settles when banks are closed. OCC rules land Jan 2027. Visa-Mesh reaches 175M merchants. Stablecoins are not winning on crypto-ness, they're winning on Sunday. $CRCL $V
items.tweetB: Lending vaults went from $4B to $10B+ in under two years while 82 projects shut down. Crypto is bifurcating into yield plumbing and dead tokens.

items.title: Strategy holds 848,517 BTC but spent 8.7x more buying back STRC preferred than buying BTC that day

items.tweetB: ETH staking is at a record and exits are almost matching entries. A record number with flat net flow is a mature stake, not a growing one. Watch the exit queue, not the headline.

items.title: France's 31.4% crypto-to-stablecoin swap tax advanced 38-37 with 100 of 577 MPs present
items.idea: France's 31.4% tax on crypto-to-stablecoin swaps advanced after MPs voted 38 to 37, with only 100 of 577 lawmakers in the room. Switzerland approved its first spot Bitcoin ETF for retail. items.angle: A 31.4% levy passed by one vote with 17% attendance. Regulatory arbitrage in the EU is a function of who shows up.
items.tweetA: France moved a 31.4% tax on crypto to stablecoin swaps. Vote: 38 to 37. Attendance: 100 of 577. A one-vote margin in an empty room just set the cost of moving onto regulated rails in France. $USDC
items.tweetB: Phantom earned $27M in builder-code fees from $50B in perps volume: 5.4bp. Wallets are becoming exchanges, and the margin is in routing.

items.title: DeepSeek V4.1-Flash scores 77% on DeepSWE 1.1, open-sources DeepInfer, reportedly raises ~$15B
items.idea: DeepSeek shipped V4.1-Flash-1017 (77% on DeepSWE 1.1), open-sourced its DeepInfer inference stack, and reportedly raised about $15B. OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra Pro runs multiple agents in parallel on one task and OpenAI acquired Orchestra Bio. Meta's Muse passed 10M US downloads in 40 days; Meta published Muse Glimmer, a 30B open-weight model that runs on a single consumer GPU.
items.angle: Open-weight models are shipping at consumer-GPU scale while the lab-level raise sizes hit $15B. Distribution wars.
items.tweetA: DeepSeek raised ~$15B, open-sourced its inference stack, and scored 77% on a software benchmark. A 30B Meta model fits on a single consumer GPU. Closed-model moats have a shelf life measured in months. $NVDA $META
items.tweetB: A $15B raise by a lab whose models are open is the weirdest business model in tech. The inference stack is the product, not the weights.

items.title: First: patient treated with AI-designed viruses for an antibiotic-resistant E. coli infection
items.idea: A patient was treated with AI-designed viruses (bacteriophage therapy) for an antibiotic-resistant E. coli infection - described as a first in medicine. Separately, a team of mostly non-scientists designed protein binders against scorpion toxins using Claude (Citrini Research's 'Citrini Therapeutics'). OpenAI acquired Orchestra Bio.
items.angle: AI-designed biologics reaching a patient is a 2026 data point on the 'AI for science' curve, and non-scientists doing protein design is the access curve.
items.tweetA: An AI-designed virus treated an antibiotic-resistant E. coli infection in a human. Mostly non-scientists used Claude to design binders for scorpion toxin. Biotech's barrier to entry is falling and nobody is pricing that into pharma R&D budgets.
items.tweetB: If a team of non-scientists can design protein binders, then the scarce input in biotech isn't design anymore. It's trials, manufacturing and regulatory. That's where the moats move.

items.title: Staples +11.1% through 16 days: third-best start to a month since 1990; the sector is 0.26% from a record

items.tweetA: Staples: +11.1% in 16 trading days, third-best month-start since 1990. Then look at the tech selloff the same day. This is the rotation. Historically the week after is flat to down, the year after is +12%. $XLP
items.tweetB: Defensives at a record high while junk yields hit 3-year highs. The market's two safest assets disagree on how scared to be.

items.title: Altman's three AI endgames: international watchdog, a CERN-style merger of labs, or one lab wins via recursive self-improvement
items.idea: The Information reports Altman laid out three scenarios at an OpenAI all-hands: (1) an international watchdog like for nuclear facilities, (2) all big labs merge into one CERN-like entity, (3) one lab reaches recursive self-improvement first and destroys everyone else's ability to compete. Guests Jaleh Rezaei and Alex Cheema argue RSI in the next few years is not a sure thing and ask if this is regulatory capture or genuine fear.
items.angle: Two of the three endgames are consolidation. Option 3 is winner-take-all. All three are inconsistent with a 17x multiple on a basket of 'competing' AI suppliers.
items.tweetA: Altman's three endgames: nuclear-style watchdog, merge every lab into a CERN, or one lab self-improves and kills the rest. Two of three end with fewer labs. Which one is your AI basket priced for?
items.tweetB: 'Which option do I prefer' is a regulation question. 'Which option is my portfolio exposed to' is a market question. If it's option 3, all the circular financing in this build-out sits on the wrong side.

items.title: US bans DeepSeek (DHS order); Nvidia can't keep up with Chinese inference chip demand
items.idea: The federal government is banning DeepSeek (DHS order in the Federal Register). Also on the show: Nvidia can't keep up with Chinese demand for inference chips; ElevenLabs voice-cloning controversy (Chris Williamson allegation, Archer voice actor response); Exo turns 4 Mac Studios into a 4.8TB/s AI cluster; looking for backdoors in Jane Street LLMs (LessWrong).
items.angle: Ban on the model and unmet Chinese chip demand at the same time. Trade policy and demand pull in opposite directions.
items.tweetA: The US bans DeepSeek on the same week reports say Nvidia can't supply China's demand for inference chips. Washington is blocking the software and the hardware still ships. The ban is on the model, not the compute. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Exo clusters 4 Mac Studios into a 4.8TB/s system. The 'you need a datacenter' assumption keeps shrinking. Inference is moving toward the edge faster than the capex is.

items.title: McKinsey explainer: forward-deployed engineers - 'may be a buzzword for what consulting firms always offered'
items.idea: McKinsey's Holger Hurtgen, Martin Harrysson and Nick Robson explain forward-deployed engineers (FDEs): engineers embedded inside a client's systems and data to build software alongside users. Interest has surged as companies try to get value from AI; the three agree FDEs help tailor AI to specific problems but disagree on how an FDE differs from a traditional consultant, so the role is still evolving.
items.angle: AI deployment is a services problem. The value isn't in the model; it's in the integration.
items.tweetA: McKinsey is explaining 'forward-deployed engineer' as if it's new. It's what Palantir has run for 15 years. The job title is spreading because model access is now commodity and integration isn't.
items.tweetB: If every AI vendor needs embedded engineers, the margin structure of AI looks like services, not software. That doesn't fit a software multiple.

items.title: McKinsey Institute: 'next $2 trillion of US-Latin America trade' and Latino-owned business growth
items.idea: McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility research: distinctive capabilities of Latino business owners and consumers in the US could drive significant growth in one of the world's biggest economic corridors (the next $2 trillion of US-Latin America trade); '5 ways to drive economic value'. 'Also consider': Latin America's productivity opportunity, and Geopolitics and the geometry of global trade: 2026 update. (Email body is a summary; full report on site.)
items.angle: A nearshoring/demographic angle on tariffs. Worth reading next to the cyberattacks on LatAm banks and mixed US trade policy.
items.tweetA: McKinsey thinks the next $2T of US-LatAm trade is carried by Latino business owners in the US. In a tariff regime that raised goods costs, a diaspora-run trade channel is the one that doesn't need a treaty. $EWW
items.tweetB: The same corridor has 400+ banks hit by AI-automated attacks this week. A $2T trade opportunity with a cyber problem is the part of the report not in the summary.
